title: The 300-HP Lexus Q-Ship Hiding A Bulletproof V8 Under Anonymous Sheetmetal - HotCars
content: By the late 1990s, Japanese brands had mastered the art of creating cars that were more than met the eye. Their European competitors were going big and bold, setting out their stall for what type of audience this car was going for. But Japanese luxury was more understated, quiet, and subtle. Sophisticated engineering, powerful engines, and surprising capability could all be hidden underneath more ordinary styling, creating a contrast between performance and appearance. But for those who knew, there was an exciting car underneath. By the late 1990s, Japanese automakers had spent years proving that they could match European manufacturers’ quality and technology. European brands like     Mercedes-Benz and BMW had built sportier models with reputations for aggressive styling and impressive performance — cars like the BMW E46 M3, E39 M5, or Mercedes-Benz E55 AMG — while Lexus instead focused more on subtlety, restraint, and a more anonymous aesthetic. This philosophy was very evident in the luxury sedan market. Where BMW and Mercedes-Benz's offerings would attract attention wherever they went, Lexus more commonly flew under the radar despite packing sophisticated engineering and, increasingly, powerful V8s under their hoods. It was a stark difference to their European counterparts, and helped to create something exciting: sleepers. Quiet confidence is what a sleeper is all about. It's knowing that you have far more power and capability than you let on, safe in the knowledge that you could deploy it whenever you wanted. And while European brands favored stylistic choices that announced their power, Lexus was comfortable obscuring theirs under unassuming bodywork and conservative exterior choices. In doing so, they created something far more interesting. For some, there’s always been something compelling about a car that hides its true potential. Something that doesn’t look as fast as it truly is. And during the late 1990s/early 2000s, cars were definitely trying to look every bit as quick as they were. Big wings, flared arches, and loud exhausts were the order of the day. But sleepers deliberately went in the opposite direction, blending into traffic and letting their performance do the talking. This was also a perfect option for executive, luxury sedans. Their restrained styling and business-like demeanor meant that a driver could have both comfort and power, should they want it, while the untrained eye would look over the car with no indication of what it was capable of. And while some brands opted for this method, it was Lexus that was arguably the best at it. The Japanese brand’s cars were never the showiest, nor the loudest, but the V8 engines they concealed gave them an intriguing personality. They were more than happy to provide refinement and elegance when required, while also quietly providing straight-line speed that would make many performance cars blush. And there was one car that did this with devastating efficiency. The first-generation GS, which was Lexus’ answer to the European executive sedan and was known as the Toyota Aristo in Japan, arrived in the early 1990s. Designed by Italdesign Giugiaro, it was a good if not particularly sporty alternative. The second generation refined the formula, improving on the chassis and bringing in the 430 nameplate, though the car remained somewhat easy to overlook in a crowded marketplace. But by the third generation, the car had come into its own. It started with the chassis. The S190 chassis used in the third-gen GS 430 was more rigid than its predecessor, had a more sophisticated suspension setup (using double-wishbones rather than the MacPherson struts), and allowed for a greater rear-wheel-drive balance. But the chassis was only part of the equation, and another crucial improvement came in the car’s engine. The 4.3-liter 3UZ-FE V8 provided 300 horsepower and 325 lb-ft of torque at a time when competing cars like the E39 BMW 540i made around 282 hp and 325 lb-ft. Power was, naturally, sent exclusively to the rear wheels, which gave it a decidedly more sporting edge than one might have expected. The car wasn't exactly a lightweight, coming in at over 3,700 pounds, but it could still hit 60 mph in 6.0 seconds en route to an electronically limited 155 mph. And it did all this while wearing the sheet metal of a sensible banker, rather than a dominating performance vehicle. The car’s aesthetic was one of what Lexus called “L-finesse”, or “Leading-Edge Finesse”. A corporate design philosophy, it aimed to turn Lexus cars from their traditionally understated designs into something far bolder and more modern. It prioritized simplicity, elegance, and a driver-first approach that tried to place controls in positions that were instinctive to the driver. The third-generation GS 430 was the first production car to employ this new take, with elements like the sloping roofline and stance aimed squarely at its European contemporaries. The wood veneer and touchscreens on the interior offered improved ergonomics to the driver, too, placing them at the center of the driving experience. It made for the     ultimate sleeper. People looking in their rearview mirror and seeing a GS 430 might presume that it wouldn't be able to keep up, but would soon be surprised as the unassuming sedan not only blasted past, but did so with its driver seated in luxurious comfort. But while the interior was good, it was the engine that was the real star of the show. Being a subsidiary of Toyota, the Lexus engineers didn’t need to reinvent the wheel when it came to powering the third-gen GS 430. They simply took one of the most proven engines in Toyota's arsenal — the 3UZ-FE — and deployed it with devastating efficiency. A naturally-aspirated V8, it came from the already-popular UZ lineup and had been popular in the LS 430. Its aluminum block helped to keep weight down, while dual overhead cams and Variable Valve Timing with Intelligence (VVT-i) allowed it to benefit from Toyota’s hard-earned reputation for reliability. Being NA also meant that power delivery was immediate and predictable, as there was no waiting for turbos to spool or superchargers to work after asking the throttle for more. This was important, because the car wasn’t designed to be a stripped-back performance machine: it was supposed to be ready to both cruise effortlessly between meetings and then eat up back roads, depending on what the day called for. That dual-purpose character was what the car was made for, and which made it the executive sedan sleeper icon it is today. The GS 430 never gained the mainstream success of cars like the BMW 5 Series or the Mercedes-Benz E-Class. And that’s arguably part of its charm. It’s a hidden gem among car enthusiasts, a V-8-powered monster without the additional drama. The car also laid the foundations for the continuation of Lexus’ V-8 GS lineage, and the L-Finesse philosophy. The GS 460 would iterate on what the GS 430 started, taking power up to 342 hp and adding an eight-speed automatic transmission compared to the GS 430's six. But the GS 430 was the one that started it. Today, the car remains an affordable, reliable, discreet option for those who know what they’re looking at. It’s not going to generate the most attention, but it’s not supposed to. It does the job, and it does it very well. We want to hear from you. title: New Midsize GS Spied: Is BMW Resurrecting The F650GS Dakar? - ADV Pulse
content: BMW Motorrad is working on a new midsize GS, recently spotted in prototype form. The move follows the launch of the F 450 GS at EICMA 2025, which replaced the G 310 GS and marked a fresh start for BMW’s entry‑level adventure lineup. Reports from Europe indicate BMW is benchmarking the new bike against Honda’s Transalp and Yamaha’s Ténéré 700, using both as development yardsticks. At the same time, BMW’s partner TVS — which builds the F 450 GS in India — already supplies a revised version of the parallel twin to Norton for its Atlas models. That engine comes in at 585 cc and produces 70 horsepower. The prototype GS seems to borrow some of that engine’s DNA, yet the Atlas has differences that raise questions about how BMW will configure the motor. One of the most notable distinctions lies in the crankshaft design. Norton’s twin uses the class‑standard 270‑degree firing order, while the F 450 GS runs with an unconventional 135‑degree crankpin offset. Whether BMW will carry that unusual setup into the midsize GS remains to be seen. As for output, expectations point to somewhere around 70 hp, keeping it below the F 900 GS’s 105 hp but right in the mix with other midsize adventure machines. Weight will likely slot in between the F 450 GS and F 900 GS at around 450 pounds wet. The chassis points to a steel bridge frame that looks closer to the F 900 GS than the entry‑level sibling, with braking components borrowed from larger models. Tubeless cross-spoke wheel sizes — 21 inches up front and 18 inches at the rear — reinforce its off‑road intent. Ample ground clearance also points to a longer-travel suspension in the 9-inch range. The bodywork still shows signs of early development, yet some design cues are already taking shape. The headlight appears inspired by the R1300 GS, though the trademark GS beak has not yet been added. The overall proportions and profile are reminiscent of the Yamaha Tenere 700, which is the model BMW is clearly aiming its sights at. Naming also remains unknown. “F 600 GS” would fit neatly into BMW’s current scheme, while reviving the “F 650 GS” badge is another possibility. For many riders, the idea of a modern take on the old F 650 GS Dakar from the early 2000s would add an extra layer of intrigue, which could be a way BMW might connect past heritage with its future midsize offering. And as history has shown, actual displacement may not be the deciding factor — past GS models like the F 800 and F 900 GS share the same displacement (895cc) despite their different names. It’s also possible BMW will remove the current F 800 GS from the lineup once this model is launched. What’s clear is that BMW still has plenty of work ahead. A production‑ready midsize GS isn’t expected before 2028, but the prototype signals BMW’s intent to strengthen its hand in one of the most competitive segments of the adventure market. title: Karol G 'marriage proposal': Her reaction made the moment even better - HOLA
content: Karol G has been collecting unforgettable fan moments on her latest tour, but a 56-year-old concertgoer may have just delivered one of the boldest yet. During the Colombian superstar's third Los Angeles concert at SoFi Stadium on Sunday, Aug. 16, a fan decided that seeing Karol G perform wasn't enough. He apparently came prepared to shoot his shot with a marriage proposal. The playful exchange was captured on video and shared across social media, including an Instagram Reel describing the concertgoer as a 56-year-old fan who proposed marriage to the singer. Other posts circulating the clip identified him as a "56-year-old Gringo fan" who described himself as "single and available."  And Karol G's reaction made the moment even better. The surprise proposal happened during the final night of Karol G's three-concert run at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California. SoFi Stadium's official schedule confirms that Karol G was booked for three consecutive shows on Aug. 14, 15 and 16 as part of her Viajando Por El Mundo Tropitour, with the Aug. 16 performance beginning at 7 p.m. It was during that third show that the 56-year-old fan caught Karol G's attention. In clips circulating on Instagram, the concertgoer is identified as being 56 and "single and available," turning his interaction with the singer into what amounted to a very public dating application. The original Reel shared by entertainment account Desde La Curva describes the encounter as Karol G receiving a "propuesta de matrimonio," or marriage proposal, from the 56-year-old fan. Other accounts quickly picked up the moment, with one post declaring: "Un fan de 56 años le pidió matrimonio a Karol G en pleno show," meaning, "A 56-year-old fan asked Karol G to marry him in the middle of the show." This was not exactly a private candlelit proposal. Thousands of people were watching. Rather than brushing off the unexpected proposition, Karol G appeared amused by the exchange. The viral posts surrounding the moment emphasize the fan's declaration that he was "single and available," while footage and reposts show the singer engaging with him from the stage. Earlier this year, the 35-year-old singer discussed her relationship status and her thoughts on marriage and children following reports that she and Feid had ended their relationship. Karol G has also previously revealed that when it comes to an actual marriage proposal, the moment matters more to her than the ring. During a dating-themed interview, she was asked what she would do if a boyfriend proposed with a ring she hated. "I don't care," Karol G responded, explaining, "I care more about the moment when he asked me." As for her ideal proposal? "A really unique one," she said as reported by DailyMotion. "Be creative." Well, proposing from the audience of a packed SoFi Stadium certainly checks the "unique" box. Whether it checks any of the others is another question. The proposal is the latest in a growing collection of unpredictable interactions between Karol G and her fans during Viajando Por El Mundo Tropitour. The tour officially began July 24 at Chicago's Soldier Field. During that opening concert, Karol G spotted another relationship-themed sign in the audience, this time from a pair of newlyweds. Their message read, "Nos casamos. Queremos ir a otro show de luna de miel," which translates to, "We got married. We want to go to another show for our honeymoon." Karol G didn't simply congratulate them. After asking where they wanted to go, the singer offered to send the couple to Paris to attend another Tropitour concert. "Nos vamos de luna de miel para París y a ver el show de Karol G," she told them, meaning they were going to Paris for their honeymoon and to see her show. The Los Angeles concerts have produced their own headline-making moments. The first SoFi Stadium show on Aug. 14 launched a three-night run, while the second featured a surprise appearance from Bruno Mars for the live debut of their collaboration "Still." © ¡HOLA! title: Jungle justice: Lawyer, group commend I-G’s directive, say practice invites anarchy - Realnews Magazine
content: A security advocacy group, the Security Situation Room (SSR), has backed the Inspector-General of Police (I-G), Mr Olatunji Disu’s directive to treat jungle justice as homicide. The group described mob action as an invitation to anarchy, saying perpetrators of extra-judicial killings must be held accountable for their actions. The President of SSR, Mr Douglas Ogbankwa, told the News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) in an interview that the directive was timely, considering the spate of mob attacks and extra-judicial killings in the country. “Of course, this directive is timely. Allowing people to resort to strong-arm tactics in solving criminal activities is an invitation to anarchy. “It is like taking the country to the Hobbesian state of nature, where life was nasty, brutish and short,” he said. Ogbankwa said the existence of government could be traced to the social contract theory, under which citizens surrendered certain liberties to enable constituted authorities to govern and protect them. He said allowing individuals to take the law into their hands would undermine the purpose of government and the rule of law. “The reason we have a government is traceable to the social contract theory, where the people agree to have people who will govern, protect them and take care of their welfare. “So, if individuals are allowed to have the liberty of taking the law into their hands, then that is simply taking us to the Stone Age without laws,” he said. The convener noted that every society was governed by laws, adding that the 1999 Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria (as amended) provided lawful avenues for resolving grievances. He said the Police Act 2020 empowered the police to detect and investigate crimes and arrest those suspected of committing offences within their jurisdiction. Ogbankwa consequently called for strict adherence to the I-G’s directive, adding that individuals must learn to be personally accountable for their actions or inactions. NAN reports that Disu directed Commissioners of Police across the 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory (FCT) to treat cases of jungle justice as homicide. Disu gave the directive on Wednesday while speaking on a live television programme on African Independent Television (AIT). The police boss condemned the growing incidence of mob attacks and extra-judicial killings across the country, describing jungle justice as murder and a violation of victims’ fundamental rights. He consequently directed the arrest and prosecution of perpetrators of jungle justice. NAN reports that Disu noted that Sections 33, 34 and 36 of the 1999 Constitution guarantee every Nigerian, including suspects, the rights to life, dignity and a fair hearing. He added that no individual or group had the authority to determine the guilt of a suspect, as the law presumes every person innocent until proven guilty by a competent court. Also speaking with NAN, a Lagos-based lawyer, Mr Ademola Owolabi of Adetokunbo Ademola Chambers, Apapa, backed the directive, saying it was legally justified. Owolabi said the law was certain but not static, adding that it was a dynamic organ that must adapt to changes in society. According to him, homicide presupposes mens rea (guilty mind) and actus reus (guilty act), noting that jungle justice might not easily fit the premeditated essence of murder. He, however, said the theory of law was that a person intended the natural consequences of his actions. “If a mob chased an alleged thief, tied tyres around his neck and set him on fire, resulting in his death, they intended to kill him. “Similarly, where planks were used to beat an alleged thief and death occurred, it is obvious that the intention was to kill,” he said. Owolabi, therefore, said the I-G was right in directing the police to treat cases of jungle justice as homicide. He, however, urged the police to embrace forensic investigation to strengthen the prosecution of such cases. According to him, cases should not be charged to court solely on the basis of confessional statements, particularly where such statements appeared to have been obtained through coercion. He said where there was evidence that a mob caught an alleged criminal but refused to hand him over to the police, members of the mob could be charged with homicide. title: Locality Pay: Why A GS-13 In San Francisco Earns About $30,000 More Than "Rest Of U.S." - fedsmith.com
content: 2026 federal locality pay supplements range from 17.06% to 46.34%. See how it affects GS-13 salaries, high-3 averages, and annuities across top and bottom areas. Calculating federal pay (Photo by Ian Smith/FedSmith; edited with AI) Federal employees under the General Schedule receive a base salary plus a locality payment that varies by geographic area. The 2026 rates range from 17.06% in the Rest of U.S. locality pay area to 46.34% in the San Jose-San Francisco-Oakland, CA, locality pay area. The federal locality pay system adjusts General Schedule salaries to reflect differences in non-federal pay levels across geographic regions. Authorized by the Federal Employees Pay Comparability Act of 1990, the system took effect in January 1994. Its purpose is to reduce pay disparities between federal and non-federal workers performing similar work in the same labor market. Locality payments are calculated as a percentage of base pay and applied according to the employee’s official worksite. The Office of Personnel Management publishes annual tables that incorporate both the across-the-board base pay increase and the locality adjustment for each designated area. For 2026, locality pay percentages remain at the prior year’s levels, while base pay received a 1.0% across-the-board increase. A locality pay area is a geographic region where federal employees receive an additional percentage adjustment. The President’s Pay Agent defines these areas after receiving recommendations from the Federal Salary Council. The Bureau of Labor Statistics supplies the underlying data by comparing General Schedule pay with non-federal compensation at comparable work levels. The cost of living is not a direct factor in the calculations. Pay disparity between federal and non-federal salaries is the primary driver. As of 2026, there are still 58 locality pay areas, including separate areas for Alaska and Hawaii and the residual Rest of U.S. category. These percentage differences compound over time. Prior FedSmith reporting has shown how cumulative annual differences of even 2–3 percentage points can produce salary gaps exceeding $20,000 at mid-level grades within a five-to-seven-year span. The five-year cumulative column assumes the 2026 rates remain constant for illustration. Actual future rates will vary with annual adjustments, but the table demonstrates the scale of the ongoing differential. An employee in the San Jose-San Francisco-Oakland area receives nearly $30,000 more per year than a counterpart in the Rest of U.S. area at the identical grade and step. Over five years, that gap exceeds $149,000 before taxes or benefits. Because locality pay is added to base pay, employees in high-rate areas receive higher total compensation for the same grade and step. The system therefore produces clear winners and losers in absolute salary terms. Employees stationed in the San Francisco Bay Area or New York metropolitan region benefit from the largest adjustments. Those in the Rest of U.S. category, which still covers a sizable share of the workforce, receive the smallest supplements. The expansion of locality pay areas has narrowed the Rest of U.S. share over the past decade. New areas created in recent years moved thousands of employees out of the residual category and into higher-rate tables. Once an area is designated, subsequent annual adjustments continue to reflect local pay disparities measured by the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Locality pay counts as basic pay for several major benefits. According to Office of Personnel Management guidance on administering locality rates, the locality-adjusted rate is used to compute retirement deductions and benefits, life insurance premiums and benefits, premium pay, severance pay, and lump-sum payments for annual leave. This treatment means that employees in higher-locality areas contribute more to the Federal Employees Retirement System and the Civil Service Retirement System due to their higher salaries. They also receive correspondingly higher life insurance coverage under the Federal Employees’ Group Life Insurance program when coverage is tied to annual basic pay. The high-3 average salary used to calculate Federal Employees Retirement System and Civil Service Retirement System annuities includes locality pay. An employee’s three highest consecutive years of basic pay, including the applicable locality percentages, form the base for the annuity formula. Because locality rates differ by location, two employees with identical grades, steps, and years of service can retire with different monthly annuities solely because of the locality rates applied during their high-3 period. Using the 2026 GS-13, Step 5 figures, the average high-3 difference between the top-10 and bottom-10 locality areas is nearly $18,000. Under the standard Federal Employees Retirement System formula—1% of high-3 multiplied by years of service (or 1.1% for employees retiring at age 62 or later with 20 or more years)—that salary gap produces a permanent difference in the annual annuity, measured in thousands of dollars. The high-3 period is not required to be the final three years of service. If an employee worked earlier in a higher-locality area, those earlier years may form the high-3 if they produce a larger average. Conversely, transferring to a lower-locality area in the final years of a career can lock in a lower high-3 if the recent lower rates become the highest consecutive three-year average. Once the annuity is computed, the benefit is fixed and is not reduced if the retiree later moves to a lower-cost area. This means that locality pay flows directly into the high-3 average salary used to compute CSRS and FERS basic annuities. High-3 is the average of an employee’s highest three consecutive years of basic pay. For most GS employees, locality-adjusted basic pay is included. A career spent primarily in a high-percentage locality, or a late-career move into one, raises the final three years and produces a higher annuity for life. The reverse—moving to a lower-percentage area near retirement—can lower the high-3 if those years end up being the highest three. The location where an employee lives after retirement does not affect the already-computed annuity. Some employees, therefore, work in high-locality areas to maximize the high-3, then relocate to lower-cost areas. TSP contributions are also based on the higher basic pay, so higher locality pay can support larger retirement savings, though individual contribution rates and investment performance remain the primary drivers. The locality pay system continues to evolve through Federal Salary Council recommendations and presidential decisions on annual adjustments. For 2026, the published rates and area definitions remain the operative figures for salary determination, benefit calculations, and retirement planning. President Trump is expected to issue an Alternative Pay Plan for the 2027 pay rates before September 1. Presidents typically issue these plans late in the month. Expectations for a 2027 civilian pay raise remain low. A few months ago, the administration released its FY 2027 budget proposal. It had no mention of a raise for federal civilian employees. The Office of Management and Budget later confirmed that the proposal effectively calls for no pay increase. By contrast, the budget does include a military pay raise, described as follows: Pay Raise for the Troops. The Administration recognizes the importance of America’s warfighters and their families, so the Budget funds a military pay raise of seven percent for all DoD (Department of War) military personnel ranked E-5 and below, six percent for E-6 to O-3, and five percent for O-4 and above. This enduring investment, far above the standard annual military pay raise, builds on the President’s recruiting and retention success, by doubling down on the Administration’s goal to restore America’s fighting force. This mirrors last year’s process. The FY 2026 budget proposal also omitted a civilian raise. The subsequent alternative pay plan provided a 1% across-the-board increase and no locality pay increase for most employees (with higher adjustments for certain law enforcement personnel). A similar alternative pay plan is possible this year. If any civilian raise materializes—whether across-the-board only or with a locality component—it is likely to be relatively small. As of mid-August 2026, Congress has not advanced language that would override a low or zero civilian increase. Federal employees in locality pay areas will continue to earn more than those in the Rest of U.S. schedule. Wi-Fi Spec: BE18000Number of Antennas/Removable: 8/NoPorts: Input WAN – One 2.5 Gbps WAN; Seven 2.5Gbps LAN; USB 3.0 (Gen 1)Processor/Memory/Storage: Quad-core 2.0 GHz/2GB/256 MBWi-Fi chips: Broadcom BCM6766802.11be performance: 2.354 Gbps (at 15 feet)Range: 130 feetSize: 8.9 x 8.9 x 3.5 inchesEstimated Annual Electricity Cost: $27.13 At $400, Asus resets the bar for high performance gaming routers with its ROG Strix GS-BE18000. Its appearance may be plain Jane but the GS-BE18000 could be the year’s stealth gaming router with everything needed to battle the world on your terms. From top triband Wi-Fi 7 speeds to access to gaming accelerators to 8 networking ports, it separates itself from the rest of the best Wi-Fi 7 routers. Among the first to implement Automated Frequency Coordination (AFC), it features better speed, range and reliability than competitors. It doesn’t matter if you’re a Leaguer or Minecrafter, the ROG Strix GS-BE18000 is not only small and modestly priced but has the power to blast your gaming into another dimension. Read on to see if this is the best gaming router for your battlestation. With a list price of $450, it pays to shop around for the Asus ROG Strix GS-BE18000. It’s available at Best Buy for $400, making it an excellent bargain that can outperform and outplay routers selling for hundreds more. The slightly less powerful ROG Strix GS-BE12000 also sells for $350 at Walmart. Considering all the Asus ROG Strix GS-BE18000 can do, it is amazing that it is roughly the size of a shoe box at 8.9 x 8.9 x 3.4 inches. That’s less than one quarter the size of the company’s ROG Rapture GT-BE19000AI router with its eight antennas pointing every which way. Available only in black, the ROG Strix GS-BE18000 is anything but intimidating looking. In fact, its boxy appearance is high on the Meh scale and not what I expect when it comes to a fire-breathing gaming router. Still, it’s what’s inside that counts, starting with Broadcom’s BCM6766 Wi-Fi chip, a 2.0GHz quad-core processor, 2GB of RAM and 256MB of flash storage for the device’s firmware and settings. It lacks the dedicated AI hardware that graces the GT-BE19000AI router, though this 8-stream router takes advantage of 320MHz data channels, Multi-Link Operations (MLO) and 4K Quadrature Amplitude Modulation (QAM). Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips. It’s among the first to tap into the higher transmission power available through 6GHz Automated Frequency Coordination (AFC) for faster data speeds, longer range and higher reliability. Using AFC is rare today and only works in the U.S., Canada, U.K. and Saudi Arabia. Look for the circle to widen over time. Able to work on all three Wi-Fi 7 bands, the GS-BE18000 features 4X4 streaming for the 5.0 and 6.0GHz transmissions, while the 2.4 GHz band is limited to 2X2 action. It adds up to a throughput rating of 18.0 Gbps. All the router’s networking ports can handle 2.5 Gbps wired traffic. In addition to the input WAN port, the GS-BE18000 has a generous seven downstream LAN connections. There’s also a Gen 1 USB 3.0 port for running a print server, making the contents of a data drive active across the LAN or using a mobile phone as a backup Internet feed when your broadband goes south. In the back are buttons for using the Wi-Fi Protected Setup (WPS) for quickie client connections and turning the router on or off. It can run as a Wi-Fi router, wired access point or a wireless node in an AiMesh network. Its excellent Quality of Service protocol is integrated into the gaming features for top access to data. It may lack the GT-BE19000AI’s window to see its components inside, but the GS-BE18000 has the router’s key specs embossed on a raised strip. There’s no info screen although its LEDs light up the ROG logo in any of seven visual effects and choice of color. Its pattern doesn’t change when the router goes offline but the stack of four LEDs below has indicators for WAN, WiFi, LAN and Power. Passively cooled, the GS-BE18000 has innovative nanocarbon-coated aluminum heat sink fins to transfer heat away from the router’s sensitive electronic components. It draws room air in from the bottom and expels hot air from the sides and top and peaked at 103.7 degrees Fahrenheit. The router is secured by Asus’s AIProtection security software that includes ad blocking, web filtering and malware protection. It stands out from the crowd (including Netgear’s Armor) by being a no-fee service that includes continual updates to thwart the nastiest attacks. The three-year warranty and life of product support blow away the competition. The router’s support pages have the expected set up tips and firmware downloads, but the 32-page manual seems rudimentary if you print it. Meant for online use, it has dozens of internal links for set up and operation tips. Based on extensive testing using Keysight’s IxChariot networking benchmark and my HP Envy X360 notebook, the ROG Strix GS-BE18000 zoomed past competitors, making it an excellent online companion. With the software set to simulate 10 data hungry users and the router next to the test machine, the GS-BE18000 moved 2.238 Gbps of data over Wi-Fi and 4.465 Gbps over 15 feet of Cat 7 cabling. This puts it in the upper echelon of high-performance routers. At the real-world distance of 15 feet, the GS-BE18000 delivered 2.354 Gbps of live data, putting it between the TP-Link Archer BE770 at 2.181 Gbps and the Asus ROG Rapture GS-BE19000AI at 2.580 Gbps. It’s more than enough for those with multi-gig data plans. With the router and test system 50 feet apart, the GS-BE18000 dominated at 1.354 Gbps, ahead of the Archer BE770’s 1.239 Gbps and one-third more throughput than the GT-BE19000AI’s 1.006 Gbps. At 75 feet, its 900.8 Mbps topped the Archer BE770 (at 772.1 Mbps) and the GT-BE19000AI (528.3 Mbps). Its 40.9 Mbps reading at 90 feet was more mundane and beaten by the Archer BE770’s 70.9 Mbps and the GT-BE19000AI’s 49.1 Mbps. Its 100-foot range should satisfy those living in mid-sized homes but is off the Archer BE770’s 130 feet. Finally, the GS-BE18000 moved upwards of 1.309 Gbps to a room 25 feet away. That’s among the best and shows the device’s ability to efficiently fill a home with data. During my two weeks with the GS-BE18000, it showed itself to be reliable and fast, although it left a couple dead zones in the attic and basement. While in use, it consumed 17.7 watts of electricity for an annual estimated power bill of about $27.13 if it runs all day and night and you pay the national average of 17.5 cents per kilowatt hour of electricity. By contrast, the Archer BE770 was a power hog at about $36 a year. It took 5 minutes to set the ROG Strix GS-BE18000 up using the Asus Router app. After I plugged everything in, I needed to pick a picture of the router, although nothing in the interface matched. The closest was “WiFi routers” and the process was automatic. I added names and passwords. It can all be done through the router’s online interface at asusrouter.com Like other Asus routers, the app is where to customize its settings. The home screen shows the current LED lighting effect as well as links to the current speed, the Internet connection status and the gaming goodies. Below are tabs for Devices (number of online devices without tapping), Insight (for firmware updates) and Family (for Web filtering by age group). The Settings tab has everything from Diagnostics and Gaming to QOS and Wi-Fi details. The router’s browser interface’s main page is incredibly dense. In addition to the current traffic and IP addresses, there’s the LED lighting effects too. The ROG Strix GS-Be18000’s Game Mode not only shows the current latency specs and deviation, but packet loses along the way. It can be set as the top data dog in the house, making your gaming the priority. Diehard gamers will love the global Ping map. The game accelerators can speed up the action for seven online games. They range from World of Tanks to Diablo 3. If the economy’s overpriced and everything has got you down, the Asus ROG Strix GS-BE18000 is a genuine bargain that can move data as fast or faster than devices selling for much more. In addition to a generous eight 2.5 Gbps wired networking ports, the GS-BE18000 uses the latest Wi-Fi tricks to deliver more than 2 Gbps available over Wi-Fi and includes an excellent AFC implementation for increasing the power and reach of the 6GHz band At $400, it’s money well spent on filling a home with high-speed gaming data. I just wish it would menace my gaming friends more. Brian Nadel is a freelance writer and editor who specializes in technology reporting and reviewing. title: BMW F 650 GS Spied Testing: India Launch Expected In 2028 - zigwheels.com
content: BMW Motorrad is preparing to enter a new battleground in the adventure bike segment. An early prototype has been spotted testing, and it is of a new middleweight GS. With this bike, the German bikemaker directly plans to go against the highly successful Yamaha Ténéré 700. This new model will slot into the big gap in BMW’s lineup between the new F 450 GS and the larger F 900 GS, using a new iteration of its parallel-twin engine. The upcoming motorcycle aims to attract a new set of customers by blending capabilities from across the existing GS family. While the final name is yet to be confirmed, the strategy which BMW is going for is clear. It plans to target the popular middleweight adventure category, a space where BMW currently lacks a contender. The upcoming bike’s design and hardware suggest a motorcycle that is more substantial and off-road focused than the F 450 GS but likely more accessible and lighter than the F 900 GS. Early photos of the test mule show a blend of all the familiar GS components which we have seen on various bikes. From the way the rear shock is mounted to the swingarm design, they appear similar to the smaller F 450 GS. However, the bike's overall presence is considerably more mature, rolling on proper off-road-spec tubless spoke wheels: a 21-inch front and an 17-inch rear. While the steel bridge frame and braking system seem to be derived from its bigger sibling, the F 900 GS. title: New BMW Middleweight Adventure Bike Spied Testing; Could Be the F 650 GS - BikeWale
content: Get Notifications on Latest UpdatesBMW Motorrad appears to be working on a new middleweight adventure motorcycle that could sit between the F 450 GS and F 800 GS in its global line-up. A test prototype of the motorcycle has been spotted, revealing several similarities to BMW’s existing GS models, although the production-specification details are still unclear. The motorcycle appears to use a parallel-twin engine and shares some technical elements with the recently introduced F 450 GS. However, its chassis and braking hardware are closer to BMW’s larger adventure motorcycles like the F 800 GS and the F 900 GS. The prototype rides on a 21-inch front and 18-inch rear wheel combination, suggesting it could offer stronger off-road capability. One of the biggest questions surrounding the motorcycle is its engine. Although it isn’t confirmed yet, BMW could use a heavily reworked version of the parallel-twin platform that powers the F 450 GS. BMW’s partner TVS uses a heavily revised version of this engine in the Norton Atlas, where the 585cc produces 70bhp. However, it remains unclear whether BMW’s motorcycle will use the same displacement or a different configuration. We expect a power output in the ballpark of 65bhp to 70bhp. That said, the BMW adventure bike will be a more off-road-focused model compared to the Norton Atlas. The prototype features a steel bridge frame that appears closer in design to the F 900 GS than the F 450 GS. Its braking system also appears to have been derived from the larger GS, while the 21-inch front and 18-inch rear wheels point towards genuine off-road capability. The motorcycle appears to be in the early development stage, with unfinished bodywork, especially around the fairing. That said, the X-style headlight seems to have taken inspiration from the BMW R 1300 GS, although the familiar GS beak is absent from the prototype. BMW has not revealed the motorcycle’s name. An F 600 GS nomenclature would fit if the engine displacement is around 600cc. However, BMW could also revive the F 650 GS name, which was previously used for its middleweight adventure motorcycles. Given the unfinished bodywork, the motorcycle seems to be at the nascent stage of development. As a result, a production version is likely to be launched sometime in 2028. When launched, this BMW adventure bike could rival the Yamaha Ténéré 700 and the upcoming KTM 690 Rally.

title: 3 ADV bikes I would choose over an SUV for road trips - HT Auto
content: Copyright © HT Media Limited  All rights reserved. For most people, a road trip means getting into an SUV, loading the boot and setting off towards the destination. But for someone who genuinely enjoys riding, an adventure motorcycle can make the journey far more rewarding. Modern ADVs offer the comfort, range and luggage carrying ability needed for long-distance touring plus then there is also while also giving you that feeling of freedom that you get on motorcycles. And once you move into the premium ADV segment, motorcycles such as the BMW R 1300 GS, Ducati Multistrada V4 and Triumph Tiger 1200 can offer an experience that is difficult to replicate in a four-wheeler. They have powerful engines for covering highway distances, sophisticated electronics, long-travel suspension and, importantly, the ability to handle changing road conditions. So, if I had the budget for a premium SUV purely for touring, these are the three adventure motorcycles I would consider instead. The BMW R 1300 GS Adventure is arguably the benchmark in the big adventure motorcycle segment. With its 1,300 cc boxer engine, excellent touring ergonomics, smooth automatic transmission, advanced electronics and impressive off-road capability, it manages to combine several roles into one motorcycle. It can comfortably cruise on highways, carry luggage and a pillion, while still being capable enough to tackle broken roads and trails. Features such as adaptive suspension, riding modes and cruise control further add to its long-distance touring credentials. For someone who wants one motorcycle that can do almost everything, the R 1300 GS Adventure would be hard to overlook. And let's not forget that torquey boxer engine. The Ducati Multistrada V4 takes a slightly different approach. While it has the adventure motorcycle proportions and touring ability expected from the segment, it brings a distinctly performance-oriented character to the table. Its 1,158 cc V4 engine produces 170 hp, making it significantly more exciting when the road opens up. At the same time, the Multistrada gets the comfort, electronics and practicality needed for covering hundreds of kilometres in a day. If the idea is to replace an SUV with a motorcycle without giving up the thrill of performance, the Multistrada V4 would be my pick. The Triumph Tiger 1200 would be my choice for riders who want something different; to be specific, that three-cylinder engine. It delivers plenty of performance for highway touring, while the long-travel suspension, 21-inch front wheel and shaft drive make the motorcycle well suited to rougher terrain. The Rally variants take the adventure credentials even further, with substantial ground clearance and a large 30-litre fuel tank. That makes the Tiger 1200 particularly appealing for riders planning long trips where fuel stops and road quality can both be unpredictable.

title: The Buick Muscle Car That Made More Torque Than An LS6 Chevelle - HotCars
content: There’s one Buick muscle car that’s being unfairly forgotten despite being a stout sleeper option that packs a luxury punch. The golden-era Buick actually has more torque than a Chevelle rocking LS6 power. But you would never know that based on auction values alone. The Chevelle LS6 is busy hogging the spotlight, while an unsuspecting Buick could embarrass it at stoplights. But unfortunately, when the "Dad" label is applied to tire-shredding monsters, they often get overlooked in favor of flashier options. In 1964,     General Motors imposed a corporate mandate that prevented midsize cars from using V8 engines with over 400 cubic inches, in order to cut down on internal power battles with the Corvette and to comply with increasing safety and regulatory concerns. Muscle cars were pretty dangerous and difficult to control as their popularity began to explode. But divisions like Pontiac and Chevrolet used factory loopholes and specific central office production orders, like COPO systems, to skirt around the rules. This enabled them to keep up with racing rivals from Ford and Chrysler with the ability to stuff massive blocks into smaller and lighter cars. The reluctance of divisions to give up massive amounts of V8 power by getting around the rules, as Ford and Chrysler continued to build them, proved that customer demand was there. The desire for bigger engines was taking performance-oriented buyers away from General Motors showrooms. So, in 1970, the ban was finally lifted, and suddenly Buick needed more power to remain competitive. Back in the 1960s, Buick had a reputation for being a brand that made luxury cruisers for older folks. It sort of still has that reputation today despite trying to erase it while targeting more youthful buyers with high-performance excitement. This is why the 1970 Buick GS 455 Stage 1 was built to dominate drag strips. This Buick has a 455 cubic-inch (7.5-liter) big-block V8 under the hood that delivers 360 horsepower and 510 lb-ft of torque. But these figures are widely believed to be underrated, as dyno tests reveal the actual power output to be closer to 400–415 hp and 515 lb-ft of torque. It may have been intentionally underrated to avoid insurance surcharges and corporate policies. The Stage 1 package adds a larger 2.12-inch intake and a 1.77-inch exhaust, stiffer valve springs, a more aggressive high-lift camshaft, a rejetted high-flow Rochester Quadrajet carburetor, functional hood scoops, and a Turbo Hydra-matic transmission with governor tweaks for higher shift points. It can accelerate from 0 to 60 mph in roughly 6.4 seconds and complete a quarter mile in about 13.3 seconds with a top speed of 135 mph. Meanwhile, the 1970 Chevy Chevelle 454 LS6 had a 454 cubic-inch (7.4-liter) V8 engine with 450 hp and 500 lb-ft of torque. This car reaches 60 mph in roughly 5.4 seconds with a 13.12-second quarter-mile time at 108 mph and a top speed of 140 mph. Despite having enough power to give the     Chevelle SS LS6 454 a run for its money, the Buick GS 455 Stage 1 failed to win over buyers. It was seen as underpowered in comparison, due to a factory rating of only 360 hp compared to 450 hp, despite having more torque, making it the ultimate sleeper model. Buick was still seen as a luxury brand for older, more mature buyers. Meanwhile, the Chevelle SS was heavily marketed toward younger buyers looking for high-powered thrills. It was seen as a more affordable icon with a massive pop culture presence. Plus, it was often promoted with brighter paint schemes and bold racing stripes. Both cars actually offered luxury comfort with available features such as bucket seats, deluxe steering wheels, padded dashboards, and optional rounded gauges. However, Buick took things a step further with upgraded upholstery, deep-twist carpeting, GS badging, wood-grain accents, molded door panels, armrests, and rear-seat speakers. Despite being more luxurious, the Buick GS 455 was the more affordable option with an original MSRP of $3,283. Adding the $199 Stage 1 Performance package increased the price to $3,482. After checking all the boxes for the 1970 Chevy Chevelle SS LS6 454, the starting price hovered between $3,500 and $3,800. But the base model started at $2,809. You can get big block V8 power for a much lower price in the Buick GS Stage 1 instead of the Chevelle SS LS6, even though the Buick models are harder to find. Only about 2,697 Buick GS 455 Stage 1 models were built in 1970, including 664 cars with the manual transmission and 232 convertibles. In comparison, about 4,475 1970 Chevy Chevelle SS LS6 454 models were made. Roughly 500 of the engines may have been placed in the El Camino instead. Chevrolet didn't break down individual production figures for hardtop and convertible models, and historians believe under 400 convertibles exist. Buick GS 455 Stage 1 models typically go for $45,000 to $65,000 if found in good, driving condition. These models found in excellent condition generally fetch between $75,000 and $110,000 at auction. Buick GS 455 cars in pristine quality can sell for between $130,000 and over $200,000. Convertibles and models with the manual transmission command the highest premiums. 1970 Chevy Chevelle SS 454 LS6 models in driving condition are snatched up for between $95,000 and $120,000. Examples in excellent condition cross the auction block for around $150,000 to $185,000. But models found in pristine or show-ready condition go for between $100,000 and over $250,000. title: Hear Becky G's New Album 'Baraja Bendita' - antiMusic
content: Discover moreEvents & ListingsMusic streaming serviceRock (align) Becky G releases her fifth studio album, BARAJA BENDITA, an 17-track body of work that stands as the most complete artistic statement of her career via RCA Records. The album's focus track, "CHULA," is an ode to a word that carries many meanings across Latin culture, centering on its use as a term of endearment while embracing its duality as both an expression of affection and a celebration of confidence, beauty, and "baddie" energy. Written as a singular body of work without guest features, BARAJA BENDITA finds Becky stepping fully into her own authorship, creating an album defined not by reinvention, but by wholeness. Her decision to build an entire album by herself was executed out of creative necessity, the 17 tracks showcase the world she built herself, on her own terms and with her own story-telling of what it means to be fully known. Rather than introducing a new version of herself, the project presents every version at once-allowing vulnerability and confidence, instinct and intention, to exist side by side. Grounded in the symbolism and strategy of a deck of cards, BARAJA BENDITA explores the idea of agency over chance. It's not about the hand you're dealt, but about becoming the one who deals it. Each song represents a different move, perspective, and emotional state, shifting in meaning as it unfolds within the larger narrative. Together, the songs create a world where control and unpredictability coexist, reflecting the complexity of identity while embracing every side of Becky. Throughout the project, she introduces BB as a creative signature that bridges Becky G, Rebbeca, and BARAJA BENDITA: a symbol of duality, ownership, and the freedom to exist fully without contradiction. "BARAJA BENDITA is about trusting myself enough to stop choosing between different parts of who I am," says Becky G. "For so long, people wanted to define me by one thing: one language, one sound, one version of myself. This album isn't about becoming someone new. It's about fully owning every part of who I've always been." The "2AM" VEVO Official Live Performance offers a glimpse into the visual world of Becky G's BARAJA BENDITA, bringing the song's intimate energy to life through a dreamlike setting filled with rich textures, warm tones, and layered details. This video marks the first installment of an exclusive series of performance videos rolling out over the coming weeks. Working alongside an accomplished roster of collaborators, Becky crafted an expansive sonic landscape where every track stands on its own while contributing to a cohesive emotional journey. Moving seamlessly between pop, Latin, electronic, alternative, and urban influences, BARAJA BENDITA allows every sound to serve the story rather than define it. For a firm whose fortunes are closely tied to trading flows and the pace of corporate transactions, a season that pairs record trading revenue with a pickup in dealmaking sits near the center of the narrative. The record in trading revenue reflected the vigor of activity across the firm's markets franchise, where it buys and sells securities, provides liquidity, and helps clients manage their exposures. Trading tends to flourish when markets are active and when clients have reason to transact, and this season delivered both. At the same time, the rebound in dealmaking and public listings signaled that the market for corporate transactions was reawakening after a period of restraint, giving the firm's advisory and underwriting operations more to do. Together, these developments painted a picture of a capital-markets business firing on multiple fronts. Goldman Sachs operates within the capital-markets corner of the broader financial sector, a segment populated by Wall Street banks and firms that help corporations, institutions, and governments raise money, transact in securities, and pursue mergers and acquisitions. Unlike a consumer-focused bank whose keep flows chiefly from everyday accounts and lending, a capital-markets firm earns from trading, advising on transactions, and underwriting the issuance of securities. This orientation ties its fortunes closely to the pace of market activity and the appetite of corporations to pursue deals and raise capital. The capital-markets segment moves in cycles. When markets are active and corporations are eager to transact, trading flows swell and dealmaking flourishes, lifting the firms that facilitate these activities. When conditions turn cautious, activity can ebb, and the same firms feel the slowdown. This cyclicality is a defining feature of the segment, and it explains why a season that combines record trading revenue with a rebound in dealmaking stands out so clearly. It signals that the cycle has swung toward greater activity, benefiting the firms positioned to capture it. Two engines drive much of the business at a firm like Goldman Sachs. The first is trading, the buying and selling of securities on behalf of clients and the provision of liquidity across markets. Trading revenue tends to rise when markets are active, when volatility creates a need for clients to adjust their exposures, and when transaction volumes swell. The record trading revenue this season reflected an environment in which these conditions came together, keeping the firm's markets desks busy across a range of products. The second engine is dealmaking and underwriting, the work of advising corporations on mergers and acquisitions and helping them raise money through the issuance of securities, including public listings. This engine depends on the willingness of corporations to pursue transactions and access markets, a willingness that ebbs and flows with confidence and conditions. The rebound in dealmaking and public listings this season indicated that corporate appetite was reviving after a quieter stretch, giving the firm's advisory and underwriting teams a fuller pipeline of activity. The revival of public listings in particular signaled renewed confidence among companies looking to enter the public markets. Goldman Sachs organizes its business around several interlocking activities. Its markets operation trades securities and provides liquidity across a wide range of products. Its banking operation advises corporations on transactions and underwrites the issuance of securities. It manages assets on behalf of institutions and individuals. And it has built out consumer-facing and transaction-banking activities that broaden its base. Each of these activities contributes to the whole, and together they form a diversified financial enterprise anchored in the capital markets. This structure is relevant to the season's results because the record trading revenue and the rebound in dealmaking both flow through core parts of the firm. When trading desks are active and the deal pipeline fills, the markets and banking operations both benefit, reinforcing each other. The firm's breadth across trading, advisory, underwriting, and asset management gives it several channels through which to capture a revival in capital-markets activity, and this season saw multiple channels contributing at once. The capital-markets industry has been navigating a cycle that swung from a burst of activity to a quieter stretch and, more recently, toward renewed vigor. The rebound in dealmaking and public listings this season reflected the latest turn in that cycle, as corporations grew more willing to pursue transactions and access markets. This revival benefits the Wall Street banks that facilitate such activity, and Goldman Sachs, as one of the most prominent names in the field, stood among the firms best placed to capture it. The revival of public listings carries particular significance. A healthy market for new listings signals confidence among companies seeking to enter the public arena, and it provides underwriting work for the banks that shepherd them through the process.
